context: Wilde to Edwin Strachan Morgan, [? April 1889], 16 Tite Street. Returning a manuscript with a verdict. Wilde was editing Woman's World and read a good deal of unsolicited work; this is what a courteous refusal from him looks like.
quote:
16, Tite Street, Chelsea S.W.

Dear Mr Morgan, I have lent your MS to a friend whose opinion I was anxious to have about, but will return it to you in a couple of days. I see you have a true literary touch as well as a feeling for the best things in art. Your style however seems to me sometimes wanting in reserve, balance, and sobriety — qualities essential to the best prose. These are things that are only attained by long practice. I fear that as it stands it will require revision before it is ready for publication. But you certainly have the artistic faculty.

Very sincerely yours Oscar Wilde
original_provenance: Read at HRC 2568, images 40-41 - one bifolium of 16 Tite Street paper, the second leaf numbered '2' in the top corner: image 40 shows sides 4 (left) and 1 (right), image 41 the inner opening, sides 2 and 3. Emphasis: none across the four sides, a null finding, and the volume prints no italic here either. Another hand: two pencil crosses on sides 2 and 3, one before 'of days' and one after 'in art.', in a soft grey pencil that is not the writing ink. They bracket almost exactly the sentence a reader would want to extract - 'I see you have a true literary touch as well as a feeling for the best things in art' - so they read as a dealer's or an editor's quotation marks rather than anything of Wilde's. Read with care: the strokes over 'practice' and 'publication' on side 4 are his extended t-crossbars, not underlines. Punctuation: 1044.
